strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: pushing LLM pruning beyond the commonly observed 50-70% sparsity regime.
The proposed global ADMM framing is clear and intuitive, and the paper gives a coherent critique of layer-wise reconstruction objectives as potentially limiting at high sparsity.
Empirical results are broad in model coverage, spanning OPT, Gemma, and LLaMA families from 125M to 27B parameters, with comparisons to several strong pruning baselines.
The high-sparsity perplexity results are impressive, especially for 80-90% unstructured sparsity where ELSA often dramatically outperforms existing methods.
The paper includes useful ablations on the next-token objective and objective-aware projection, plus experiments on semi-structured and non-uniform sparsity patterns.
The appendix provides substantial numerical tables and implementation details, which helps assess the results beyond the main figures.
weaknesses: The main comparison is not fully fair: ELSA performs iterative full-model optimization for 4096 steps and uses larger calibration/training sets, while many baselines are one-shot or layer-wise methods using 128 calibration sequences. The paper does not normalize for compute, data, or tuning budget, making it hard to attribute gains purely to the proposed formulation.

The claims of retaining high fidelity or pruning without significant degradation are overstated. At 90% sparsity, zero-shot accuracy remains far below dense performance, and perplexity is still several times worse than dense models, even if much better than baselines.

The method appears closer to sparse fine-tuning/retraining than pruning in the standard low-cost post-training sense, but the paper does not compare against relevant iterative pruning plus fine-tuning or sparse training baselines under matched compute.

The theoretical convergence result has limited practical force: it relies on assumptions and update conditions that do not clearly match Adam/SGD training of nonconvex LLMs, bounded iterates, quantization error conditions, and approximate x-updates used in practice. It establishes stationarity rather than a strong optimality guarantee.

Novelty is moderate rather than strong. ADMM-based pruning and global sparse optimization have substantial precedent, including L-ADMM and SparseLLM; the main contribution is a well-executed adaptation with an objective-aware projection rather than a fundamentally new optimization principle.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the code URL is absent, calibration/training data sizes for ELSA are not fully specified in the main experimental details, some hyperparameter table entries are blank or hard to interpret, and no variance across seeds is reported.

Efficiency claims are underdeveloped. The paper reports memory savings for ELSA-L but lacks systematic wall-clock time, total GPU-hour cost, pruning throughput, inference speedup, or sparse-kernel deployment results, which are central for a pruning paper.
Several presentation inconsistencies weaken confidence, including numerical mismatches between main-text claims and appendix tables and occasional overclaiming in figure captions and discussion.
The semi-structured sparsity results are not particularly strong: ELSA is often worse than the best baselines at 2:4 and 4:8 sparsity, so the adaptivity claim is only weakly supported.

strengths: Targets an important and timely problem: pushing LLM pruning beyond the commonly observed 50-70% sparsity regime.
The core idea of optimizing the language-modeling objective directly with an ADMM-style sparse constraint is natural, well motivated, and contrasts clearly with layerwise reconstruction methods.
Empirical perplexity results at 80-90% sparsity are large and consistent across several model families and sizes, especially compared with one-shot pruning baselines.
The paper includes a useful range of comparisons, downstream zero-shot evaluations, a 27B-scale low-precision variant, and some ablations on objective choice and projection.
The presentation is generally understandable, and the appendix provides many numerical results rather than only plots.
weaknesses: The main evaluation is not apples-to-apples. Most baselines are one-shot or low-calibration post-training pruning methods using 128 calibration sequences, while ELSA performs thousands of gradient-based optimization steps and uses larger, unspecified calibration/training sets. The paper does not provide equal-compute or equal-data comparisons, making the central performance claims difficult to interpret.

The strongest missing baselines are simple ones under the same budget: sparse fine-tuning with iterative magnitude pruning, projected gradient descent, ADMM without the proposed projection but with the same data/steps, or other mask-learning/sparse training baselines. Without these, it is unclear how much of the gain comes from the proposed method versus just using far more optimization and data.

Claims such as “maintaining high fidelity” and “without significant performance degradation” are overstated. At 90% sparsity, perplexity and zero-shot accuracy remain far from dense models; for example LLaMA-2-7B average zero-shot accuracy drops from about 59.7 to 38.5. This is better than baselines but not close to dense fidelity.

The paper emphasizes theoretical convergence, but the guarantee is weak relative to the claims. It only reaches a stationary point under strong assumptions, does not establish global optimality for the nonconvex sparse LLM problem, and relies on update conditions that do not match practical stochastic approximate training. The theory does not substantially explain the empirical gains.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The text says code will be made available but gives no usable link, the exact larger data counts for ELSA are not clearly specified in the main setup, hyperparameter tables appear incomplete or hard to parse, and the extent of per-model/per-sparsity tuning is unclear.

Efficiency claims are underdeveloped. Since the main results use unstructured sparsity, the paper does not show actual wall-clock inference speedups, memory savings at inference, or deployment measurements on sparse kernels. Parameter sparsity alone does not guarantee practical acceleration.

The 27B experiment is limited: it reports essentially one model and sparsity setting, omits several baselines due to feasibility, and does not fully separate the contribution of low-precision state storage from the pruning method itself.

Some auxiliary experiments weaken the broad claims. In N:M semi-structured sparsity, ELSA is not clearly competitive with the best baselines, and at lower sparsity levels it often underperforms existing methods on zero-shot accuracy.

The framing is too sweeping. The paper repeatedly suggests that previous work hit an artificial “sparsity wall,” but the evidence mainly shows that a much more expensive optimization procedure can outperform cheaper post-training methods. This is an important but narrower conclusion.

Overall, the empirical results are promising, but the evaluation design and overclaiming create serious concerns. I would not support acceptance without equal-budget comparisons, clearer reproducibility, stronger deployment evidence, and more careful positioning.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: pushing LLM pruning beyond the commonly observed 50-70% sparsity regime.
The central idea of replacing layerwise reconstruction-error pruning with a global sparsity-constrained optimization formulation is clear, well motivated, and likely useful for the pruning community.

Empirical results are strong: ELSA substantially improves perplexity at 80-90% sparsity across OPT, Gemma, LLaMA-2, and LLaMA-3.2 models, with especially large gains over SparseGPT, Wanda, ALPS, SAFE, L-ADMM, and SparseLLM in the extreme-sparsity regime.
The evaluation includes both perplexity and zero-shot task accuracy, multiple model families and scales, structured and unstructured sparsity settings, and a 27B-scale memory-efficient variant.
The ablations on next-token prediction versus reconstruction error and on objective-aware projection support the main design choices.
The paper is generally well organized and provides useful appendix tables with numerical results and hyperparameter details.
weaknesses: The comparison to many baselines is not fully apples-to-apples: ELSA performs thousands of optimization steps and uses larger calibration/training sets, while several baselines are one-shot or use only 128 calibration sequences. The paper should more explicitly quantify the extra compute/data cost and compare against stronger fine-tuning-aware baselines under matched budgets.

The practical efficiency claims are incomplete. Most results are for unstructured sparsity, but the paper does not report actual inference speedups, hardware memory savings at inference, or serving throughput/latency. High unstructured sparsity may not translate into usable acceleration without specialized kernels.

The theoretical convergence analysis is only loosely connected to the implemented method. It assumes smoothness/weak convexity, bounded iterates, exact or controlled inexact updates, and deterministic objectives, whereas the experiments use Adam, stochastic minibatches, mixed precision, schedules, and approximated projections. Thus the theory is reassuring but not strong evidence for the actual algorithm.

Some technical details are underspecified or confusing, including the exact amount of training data used by ELSA in the main experiments, the compute/runtime overhead relative to baselines, and the precise implementation of objective-aware projection from Adam second moments.
The 27B experiment is promising but limited: it appears to report only one model and one sparsity level, with few baselines due to infeasibility and no downstream task accuracy or runtime analysis.
The paper claims code will be released but the manuscript contains an incomplete placeholder, which weakens reproducibility at review time.

The method underperforms or is only competitive in some moderate-sparsity structured settings, suggesting the main advantage is concentrated in expensive global optimization at extreme unstructured sparsity rather than a uniformly better pruning method.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: pushing LLM pruning beyond the common 50-70% sparsity regime while retaining useful language modeling performance.
The empirical results are broad and compelling for unstructured sparsity, covering multiple architectures and sizes from OPT-125M to LLaMA-2-13B, with an additional 27B experiment.

Comparisons include many relevant pruning baselines such as Wanda, SparseGPT, ALPS, L-ADMM, SAFE, and SparseLLM, and the gains at 80-90% sparsity are often large in perplexity and downstream zero-shot accuracy.
The paper goes beyond perplexity by reporting zero-shot tasks, cost analysis, memory reduction, and sparse-kernel inference speedups, which makes the practical motivation stronger.
The method is conceptually simple: directly optimize the next-token objective under a sparsity constraint using ADMM-style variable splitting, with a useful objective-aware projection heuristic.
The appendix provides substantial implementation detail, including training data size, optimizer settings, sparsity schedules, hardware, and hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The main comparison is not fully apples-to-apples: ELSA uses iterative optimization over 32,768 sequences and multiple GPUs, while several baselines are one-shot or layerwise methods designed for much smaller calibration budgets. The paper partly addresses this with cost analysis and Wanda retraining, but only in a limited setting.

The central claim that ELSA preserves performance at extreme sparsity is somewhat overstated. At 90% sparsity, perplexity and zero-shot accuracy remain substantially degraded relative to dense models, even if they are much better than baselines.

The theory has limited practical force. The convergence result relies on assumptions such as weak convexity, bounded iterates, sufficiently accurate subproblem solutions, and stationarity for an idealized objective; these do not convincingly characterize modern LLM training or the implemented heuristic with Adam, diagonal Fisher estimates, schedules, and quantized states.

Novelty is meaningful but not cleanly separated from prior ADMM and global pruning work. The paper would benefit from a sharper explanation of what is fundamentally new relative to L-ADMM, SparseLLM, and standard sparse fine-tuning with projection.

The objective-aware projection is only lightly ablated. The reported ablation is narrow, and the connection between Adam second moments, diagonal Fisher, Hessian geometry, and actual pruning importance is plausible but not strongly validated.

Hardware relevance is mixed: the strongest results are for unstructured sparsity, while the N:M semi-structured results are only roughly competitive and sometimes worse than existing methods. This limits the deployment implications on common accelerators.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the source-code location appears blank in the manuscript, and the experiments are resource-intensive. Seeds, variance, and robustness across calibration/training samples are not reported.

There are several presentation and consistency issues, including minor numerical inconsistencies between narrative and appendix tables, awkward phrasing, and some overclaiming around breaking the sparsity wall and achieving high fidelity.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: obtaining practically useful high-sparsity LLMs with real memory and inference benefits.

The high-level motivation is reasonable: layer-wise reconstruction objectives can be limiting, and directly optimizing the language-modeling objective under a sparsity constraint is a plausible direction.

The reported perplexity gains at 80-90% sparsity are large across several model families and scales, especially for LLaMA-2 and OPT, and the paper includes comparisons to several relevant pruning baselines.

The paper attempts to go beyond perplexity by reporting zero-shot task accuracy, deployment-oriented latency/memory measurements, a 27B-scale experiment, and ablations for the objective and projection step.
weaknesses: The evaluation is not sufficiently fair or controlled. ELSA uses iterative optimization on 32,768 sequences, while many baselines use the standard 128-sequence one-shot calibration setup. This makes the headline comparisons against Wanda, SparseGPT, ALPS, L-ADMM, SAFE, and SparseLLM hard to interpret as method superiority rather than simply more optimization/data/compute.

The compute analysis is too narrow. A matched retraining comparison is only shown for Wanda at 90% on LLaMA-2-7B, while most main figures compare ELSA to much cheaper or qualitatively different baselines. Equal-token, equal-step, and equal-GPU-hour comparisons across stronger baselines are needed.

The downstream results are much less compelling than the perplexity narrative. At 50-60% sparsity ELSA is often not the best method, and at 90% the retained zero-shot accuracy is still far below dense performance; several tasks are near chance or dominated by dataset artifacts, weakening the claim of high model fidelity.

The theoretical section has serious issues. The paper repeatedly implies that ELSA solves the original constrained problem, but the stated result is only convergence to a lambda-stationary point under strong assumptions. Moreover, the proof appears to incorrectly treat the sparsity set S as finite, although the set of k-sparse real-valued vectors is infinite.

The ELSA-L convergence result is under-specified. The quantization operator is not modeled with clear error assumptions sufficient to justify the theorem, and the algorithm in the appendix is not clearly consistent with the method description.

The novelty is overstated. ADMM-based pruning, global sparse fine-tuning, OBS/second-order-inspired criteria, and optimizer-state-based curvature approximations are all well-established ingredients. The paper needs a sharper technical distinction from prior ADMM pruning, SparseLLM, ALPS, SAFE, and retraining-based sparse fine-tuning.

The deployment claims need more scrutiny. Unstructured sparsity speedups depend heavily on specialized kernels, hardware, batch size, sequence length, and decoding regime. The paper reports one RTX 3090 setup with MACKO, but does not establish general practical benefit or compare to quantization/structured sparsity tradeoffs.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript says code and environment details will be available but leaves placeholders, and many important choices remain unclear, including hyperparameter selection protocol, tuning budgets for baselines, mask-update details, schedules, and sensitivity to calibration data size.

Some additional experiments weaken the central story: for N:M semi-structured sparsity ELSA is only roughly on par and sometimes worse than existing methods, suggesting the proposed formulation is not broadly dominant across practical sparsity patterns.

The writing substantially oversells the findings with claims such as breaking through an 'unseen frontier' and solving the true objective, while the evidence supports a more limited conclusion: expensive global sparse optimization can improve perplexity at very high unstructured sparsity under the tested settings.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: pushing LLM pruning beyond the apparent 50-60% sparsity wall while preserving usable quality and realizing actual inference/memory gains.

The central idea of replacing layerwise reconstruction surrogates with a global sparsity-constrained objective solved by ADMM is clear, well motivated, and meaningfully positioned against current LLM pruning practice.
Empirical results are strong across several model families and scales, including OPT, Gemma, and LLaMA models from 125M to 13B, with additional evidence at 27B using the low-precision ELSA-L variant.

The gains at high sparsity are substantial: ELSA remains far more stable than Wanda, SparseGPT, ALPS, SAFE, L-ADMM, and SparseLLM in the 80-90% sparsity regime, and the paper reports both perplexity and zero-shot downstream evaluations.
The paper goes beyond quality metrics by measuring deployment-relevant benefits with sparse kernels, showing meaningful latency, throughput, and memory improvements at 90-95% sparsity.
The ablations on next-token prediction versus reconstruction error and objective-aware projection are useful and support the paper’s main design choices.
Reproducibility details are relatively extensive, including datasets, calibration/training sizes, optimizer settings, sparsity levels, hardware, and hyperparameter tables.
weaknesses: The fairness of the comparison is somewhat complicated: ELSA uses substantially more calibration/training data and iterative optimization than many one-shot baselines, so the headline comparison partly reflects a different compute/data regime, even though the cost analysis helps mitigate this concern.

Theoretical claims should be toned down or clarified. The convergence proof relies on assumptions that are not obviously satisfied by practical LLM training, and parts of the proof appear to treat the sparse constraint set as finite, which is not true for the continuous k-sparse parameter set unless one is reasoning only over supports.

The proof does not fully cover all practical algorithmic details, such as stochastic minibatch optimization, Adam/bf16 training, objective-aware Hessian/Fisher projection, schedules for the penalty parameter, and low-precision/distributed implementation effects.

Some claims about preserving model fidelity are stronger than the downstream results suggest: at 90% sparsity, zero-shot accuracy still drops substantially relative to dense models, even if ELSA is clearly better than baselines.
The paper would benefit from reporting variance over seeds or calibration samples, especially because high-sparsity pruning can be sensitive and many results are presented as single runs.
Structured N:M sparsity results are less compelling than the unstructured results; ELSA is roughly competitive but not clearly superior there, which narrows the practical hardware acceleration story.
The 27B-scale experiment is encouraging but limited to one model and one sparsity point, so the scalability claim, while plausible, is not as thoroughly established as the 7B/13B results.
